passage: Four students were failing a subject, and each tackled it differently. Amandeep, failing Maths, asked why over and over and traced the trail back to his shaky fractions and basic algebra from Class 8. The trouble was foundations, not the current chapter. Irawati stayed after class, showed the teacher her last three test papers, and agreed on two doubt sessions a week, which suited her better and cost less than joining a full extra batch. Sumit revised English and Biology since those felt pleasant. His marks in those rose a little, but Maths, skipped again, went on dragging his result down. Meera spent a month reading her notes again and again. Her scores hardly moved. She admitted that reading was not working, and switched to answering questions with the book closed, which showed her real weak spots within days.

qa.q: How many test papers did Irawati show her teacher?
qa.a: She showed her last three test papers.

qa.q: How does Sumit's choice of subjects differ from Amandeep's approach, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Sumit kept revising the subjects he liked and skipped Maths, so his result still dropped. Amandeep asked why and found weak basics from Class 8, so he knew what to fix.

qa.q: What might Sumit be feeling when he picks up English instead of Maths?
qa.a: He is probably avoiding discomfort and wants the good feeling of doing well, so Maths feels too hard to face.
He could begin with ten minutes of Maths, ask a teacher what to study first, and slowly increase the time. Starting with the easiest topic may help him face the hard ones. 🙂

grounding: Students fix a failing subject by tracing the root, asking the teacher, avoiding it, and changing the method when no improvement shows.
